IPO Listing Day Predictor, explained simply

Every section starts with a blue box that explains the idea the way you would explain it to a small child. After that come the real numbers, tables and charts. Every number in this guide comes from the project's notebooks and reports (real data, nothing made up).

Start here What is this project?

The story first, then the numbers, then the words you need.

0. The whole project in 1 minute

In simple words

Imagine a new toy shop opens and sells pieces of itself to people for the first time. That is an IPO. Each piece (a share) has a fixed price, say ₹100.

Before the shop opens, people stand in a line to buy pieces. If 100 people want a piece but only 1 piece is there for them, the line is "100 times" long. That is called subscription.

On the first day the pieces start trading on the stock market (listing day), the price can jump to ₹150 (happy!) or fall to ₹90 (sad). That jump is the listing gain.

I built a guessing machine (a machine learning model). It looks at how long the line was, who stood in it, and whether the whole market is happy or scared, and then it guesses the jump before the first day.

Then I checked: if a normal person had followed my machine for 2 years, would they have made more money than without it? Yes, a bit more, and I checked that it was not luck.

1. Collect652 real IPOs from Kaggle, NSE company list, prices from Yahoo Finance
2. Clean and checkfix names and types, drop 18 rows, verify 499 listing prices
3. Explore (EDA)subscription is the strongest signal; the market changes over time
4. Features18 inputs, all known before listing
5. Modelrandom forest, tested on years it never saw
6. Money testbacktest with the allotment lottery, then the app

3. Where the data came from

In simple words

To learn, the machine needs old examples: many past IPOs, how long each line was, and how much each one jumped on day one. I took these from three places on the internet, and I used one place to check the other, like asking two friends the same question.

QuestionPlain EnglishTechnical term
Main sourceA public dataset on Kaggle called IPO Data India 2010-2026 (uploaded by karanammithul). One row per IPO.Public Kaggle dataset, Excel file, 652 rows
Is it real?Yes. These are real Indian IPOs with their real subscription numbers and prices.Real (not synthetic) data
Second sourceNSE's own list of every company listed on it, with the listing date.EQUITY_L.csv (mainboard), SME_EQUITY_L.csv (small companies)
Third sourceYahoo Finance: the actual price on the first day, and NIFTY / VIX history.yfinance Python library
Why three sources?Kaggle has the subscription numbers but no stock symbol, and some listing prices looked wrong. NSE gives the symbol, Yahoo gives the real price to check Kaggle.Cross-validation of the target
How was it downloaded?By Python scripts. Every raw file is logged with its source, date and a fingerprint (SHA-256), so anyone can check it is the same file.data/raw/manifest.json
Anything avoided on purpose?No scraping of websites whose rules forbid it. The grey market premium (GMP) was not used: it is unofficial and its history can't be checked.Data ethics, verifiability

6. Data cleaning

In simple words

Before cooking, you wash the vegetables and throw away the rotten ones. Cleaning is the same: fix names, fix numbers, find missing pieces, and remove things that are not really IPOs.

#What I didHow (step by step)Why
1Renamed columns
  1. Issue_Size(crores) → issue_size_cr, QIB → sub_qib, and so on.
  1. Short, same-style names are easy to type and hard to mix up.
2Fixed cut-off names
  1. 69 names ended in "..." (cut off).
  2. Removed the "...".
  3. Kept a yes/no column name_truncated.
  1. The name is needed to find the NSE symbol (Section 7).
  2. The flag tells the matching step to compare only the start of the name.
3Fixed datatypes
  1. Date text → real date (pd.to_datetime).
  2. All numbers → decimal numbers (float).
  1. You can't sort by date or take an average of text.
4Duplicates
  1. df.duplicated().sum()
  2. Result: 0.
  1. A copy would count the same IPO twice.
5Missing values
  1. missing_info(df) (the class helper).
  2. 2 rows miss subscription, 2 miss listing gain: 3 IPOs in total.
  3. Dropped them (Step 8).
  1. A row with no answer (listing gain) can't teach the model anything.
  2. Guessing the answer would be inventing data.
6Outliers: checked, kept
  1. out_info(df) (IQR / z-score helper) and boxplots.
  2. It flags issue size 13.8%, HNI 12.9%, retail 12.4%, listing gain 8.4% of rows.
  3. Did not remove them.
  4. Used the log of subscription and size instead, and MAE as the score.
  1. These are not typing mistakes: a 300x IPO or Hyundai's ₹27,859 crore IPO really happened.
  2. Removing them removes exactly the IPOs that matter most.
  3. Log squeezes huge numbers so they don't dominate.
7Marked REITs / InvITs
  1. Rows with retail subscription = 0 looked odd.
  2. They were REITs / InvITs (trusts).
  3. Marked by name ("REIT", "InvIT", "Trust") or RII = 0: 14 rows.
  1. Trusts have no retail quota and different investors.
  2. Mixing them with companies would confuse the model.
8Dropped rows that don't belong
  1. 14 REITs / InvITs.
  2. 1 FPO: Vodafone Idea (2024), an already listed company.
  3. 3 rows with missing values.
  4. Total dropped: 18. Left: 634.
  1. The project is about first-time IPOs of companies.
  2. Every dropped row has its reason written in the column exclude_reason, so nothing disappears silently.
9Sorted and gave ids
  1. Sorted by date, then name.
  2. Gave every IPO an id: IPO0001, IPO0002, ...
  1. Time order matters for everything later.
  2. An id lets every file point to the same IPO.

7. Finding each IPO's NSE symbol

In simple words

To find a classmate's phone number, you look for their name in the class list. But one list says "Ravi K." and the other says "Ravikumar". So you look for the closest name, among people who joined the class in the same week.

#What I didHowWhy
1Cleaned both nameslowercase, "&" → "and", removed "Ltd", "Limited", "Pvt", "the", "IPO""Larsen & Toubro Infotech Ltd." and "Larsen and Toubro Infotech Limited" both become larsen and toubro infotech
2Only looked near the dateonly NSE companies that listed within 7 days of the Kaggle dateFewer candidates, fewer wrong matches
3Scored name similarityrapidfuzz: best of three scores (word order, start of name for cut-off names, shared words)Handles different word order and cut-off names
4Accepted only 85+score out of 100; below 85 = "unmatched"Better to have no symbol than a wrong one
5Fixed a bad match"VMS Industries" was matching "PI Industries" (shared word "industries"). Now the shared-words score only counts when the first word also matchesFound by checking the lowest-score matches by eye
547
IPOs matched to an NSE symbol
105
not matched: mostly delisted or merged companies, or BSE-only

8. Listing price and the split problem

In simple words

If you cut a pizza into 5 slices, each slice is worth one fifth. Companies do this with shares too (a split or bonus). Yahoo then quietly divides all the old prices by 5, so IRCTC's first-day price looks like ₹125 instead of ₹626. I had to multiply it back.

IPOReal listing priceWhat Yahoo showsWhyFix
IRCTC (Oct 2019)₹626about ₹1251:5 split in 2021₹125 × 5 = ₹626 again

How: for each IPO, multiply the first-day prices by every split ratio that happened after the listing day (split_factor). 90 of the 545 IPOs with a price had at least one later split or bonus, so without this fix about 1 in 6 targets would have been wrong.

Before and after the fixKaggle and NSE agreed for only about 63% of IPOs before the split fix. After the fix, 95% agree.

9. Checking Kaggle's numbers

In simple words

Two friends tell you the score of a match. If they say the same, you believe it. If they say a little different, maybe one watched another channel. If they say very different, one of them is wrong, and you go and check.

The rule: compare Kaggle's listing gain with the gain from the NSE open
DifferenceLabelMeaningIPOs (kept)
2 pp or lessagreesame price390
2 to 10 ppcloseKaggle probably used BSE's open, Yahoo has NSE's open. Fine.109
more than 10 ppdisagreeone of them is wrong26
Agree or close, out of the 525 that could be checked499 (95.0%)

Who was wrong in the 26? I checked a few by hand against news reports of the listing price: CDSL listed at ₹250, Paras Defence at ₹475, Nazara at ₹1,971, Bansal Wire at ₹352. Kaggle was right; Yahoo's split history was wrong.

So the target (the answer the model learns) is:
CaseTarget usedMarked asIPOs
agree or closegain from the NSE open (Yahoo)nse_open_yahoo499
disagree, not on NSE, no priceKaggle's listing gainkaggle_unverified135
Say it: "I didn't trust one source. I matched every IPO to its NSE symbol, fixed Yahoo's split adjustment, and 95% of Kaggle's listing prices agreed with the NSE open."

Notebooks 02_eda.ipynb and 03_feature_engineering.ipynb. 634 clean IPOs, seven findings.

11. EDA: seven findings

In simple words

Before building the guessing machine, I looked at the old IPOs with my own eyes, using tables and pictures, to see what usually happens. Each finding below became a decision for the model.

1Most IPOs list a little up; a few list hugely up

Question: How do IPOs usually list?  ·  What I did: summary numbers and a histogram of the listing gain.

MeasureValueIn plain words
Median gain6.6%the middle IPO lists 6.6% up
Mean gain16.8%the average is pulled up by a few huge winners
Skew2.5long tail on the right side
Listed below offer price25.2%1 in 4 IPOs lose money on day one
Listed flat (0%)6.3%opened exactly at the offer price
Gain above 15%34.2%1 in 3
Gain above 50%11.5%about 1 in 9
What I sawThe mean (16.8%) is 2.5 times the median (6.6%). A few hot IPOs make the "average IPO" look much better than the typical one.
What it meansUse MAE (average miss) as the main score, not RMSE, which a few 200% IPOs would dominate. And give a range, not just one number.
Say it: "The typical IPO lists 6.6% up, but 1 in 4 lists below the offer price."

What I sawOnly 4 IPOs in 2013, 102 in 2025. Median gain from −2.8% to +23.4%.
What it meansA random train/test split is wrong here: it would let the model learn from 2025 and be tested on 2019. The split must be by time: learn from old years, test on new years.

3Subscription is the strongest signal

Question: Does a longer line mean a bigger jump?  ·  What I did: grouped IPOs into subscription buckets.

Total subscriptionIPOsMedian gain% listed with a gain
less than 1x260.0%38%
1 to 3x1770.0%41%
3 to 10x1043.9%62%
10 to 30x909.9%70%

100x and more7356.6%100%
What I sawBelow 3x, less than half list with a gain. Above 30x, more than 9 in 10 do. The popular "apply only if 30x+" rule is real.
What it meansThe "bucket median" (median gain of past IPOs with the same subscription) becomes the baseline the model must beat. Subscription goes from 0.5x to 1000x+, so the model gets its log.
Say it: "Above 30x subscription, 9 in 10 IPOs list with a gain; below 3x, it's a coin toss."

4Rich individuals and institutions matter more than retail

Question: Whose line matters most?  ·  What I did: Spearman correlation (a ranking correlation that is not fooled by outliers) of each column with the gain.

ColumnCorrelation with gainIn plain words

HNI subscription0.67strong
QIB subscription0.64strong
Retail subscription0.58a bit weaker
Offer price0.03no link on its own

What I sawThe four subscription columns move together (correlation 0.64 to 0.93 with each other).
What it meansThat is multicollinearity. Tree models don't mind it; for the straight-line model, Ridge (which handles it) is used instead of plain linear regression.

6Market mood helps a little

Question: Do IPOs list better when the whole market is happy?  ·  What I did: median gain when NIFTY is above / below its 200-day average, and when recent IPOs did well / badly.

SituationMedian gain

CarefulInside the same subscription bucket the effect is mixed. Market mood is a secondary signal; the model decides how much to use it.

7Subscription numbers have inflated

Question: Does "50x" mean the same in 2012 and 2025?  ·  What I did: median gain per subscription bucket in three eras.

Subscription2010 to 20192020 to 20232024 to 2026
less than 3x−0.1%0.1%−1.0%
3 to 10x4.2%3.8%0.0%
10 to 30x11.3%12.7%6.5%
30 to 100x25.1%36.9%14.1%
100x and more59.2%75.0%36.5%
Median subscription4.9x22.6x28.0x
In simple words

When a toy is rare, a long line means it is really special. When everyone starts standing in every line, a long line means less. That is what happened: lines got 6 times longer, and the jump for the same line got about half as big.

What I sawThe typical IPO went from about 5x to about 28x subscribed, and a 100x IPO's median gain fell from 75% to 36.5%.
What it meansA model trained once and never updated will expect too much. This is why the final model is retrained every quarter (Section 14, steps 7 and 8).
Say it: "Subscription has inflated: 100x today is worth about half of 100x in 2021, so the model has to keep learning."

Summary: what EDA told the model

FindingDecision for the model
1. Long right tailMAE as the main score; also predict an 80% range
2. Good and bad yearsSplit by time, never randomly
3. Subscription is the strongest signalLog of subscription as features; bucket median as the baseline
4. HNI / QIB matter more than retailKeep all four groups plus "QIB vs retail"; Ridge for the linear model
5. Size alone says littleKeep it (log), let the model combine it
6. Market mood helps a littleAdd NIFTY, VIX and recent-IPO features
7. Subscription inflationRetrain every quarter (walk-forward)
Part 3 Features: what the model is allowed to see

Notebook 03_feature_engineering.ipynb. 18 inputs, all known before listing day.

12. The no-peeking rule

In simple words

In an exam you can't look at tomorrow's newspaper. The model has the same rule: it may only use what a person could know before the IPO lists. If it peeks at the future, it looks clever in practice and fails in real life.

The line for an IPO (subscription) closes about 3 working days before listing (T+3 rule since Dec 2023; up to 6 days before that). To be safe, every market number is taken from 7 calendar days before the listing date. That day is called the cutoff.

Day −7 (cutoff)Last day of market data the model may use
Around day −6 to −4IPO open for applications (3 working days)
About day −3Applications close, subscription numbers known; the model makes its call
Day 0Listing day. The answer. Never used as an input.

For IRCTC (listed 14 Oct 2019) the cutoff was 7 Oct 2019: NIFTY data, VIX and recent-IPO numbers are all from that day or earlier.

What is data leakage?

Leakage means the model sees something during training that it could not know in real life, usually a piece of the future. It is the most common, and the most dangerous, mistake in machine learning, because it does not show up as an error: it shows up as a score that looks too good.

If the model peeksIt scores very well in testing ("wow, so accurate"), then fails when used for real, because the future is never known in advance. Like a student who got tomorrow's answer sheet: 100/100, but learnt nothing.
With the no-peeking ruleThe testing score is lower but honest. It is the score you can expect on the next IPO, because every guess was made only from the past.

Why 7 days?

  • Since Dec 2023 an IPO lists 3 working days after applications close (the T+3 rule). Before that the gap was up to 6 days.
  • 3 working days can become 5 or 6 calendar days when a weekend or a holiday falls in between.
  • So 7 calendar days puts the cutoff before applications close for every IPO, old or new.
  • The cost: the model misses the last few days of market mood. The benefit: no future information can ever slip in. A small loss of signal is worth a score you can trust.

Every guard against leakage in this project

#What I didWhat it stops
1Market data (NIFTY, VIX) only up to the cutoff, 7 days before listingThe model seeing the market around listing day
2Dropped the CMP (BSE), CMP (NSE) and Current Gains columnsUsing today's price, which nobody knew on listing day
3"Recent IPOs" counts only IPOs that listed before the cutoffSeeing how later IPOs did
4A 7-day gap between training and validation in every year foldA test IPO's close neighbour sitting in the training data
5Walk-forward: each quarter is predicted by a model trained only on earlier IPOsAny guess being made with knowledge of later results
6Missing values filled with the median inside the pipeline, learnt from training rows onlyTest data leaking into training through the fill value
7An automated test: adding later IPOs must never change an earlier IPO's featuresFuture data creeping into past rows by mistake (a check that runs every time)
Say it: "Market data stops 7 days before listing, current-price columns are dropped, folds keep a 7-day gap, and an automated test proves that adding new IPOs never changes an old IPO's features."

Why "log"?

Lines go from 1x to 300x. If you draw 1, 10, 100 and 300 on a normal ruler, 1 and 10 are squashed together and 300 is far away. A log ruler puts them at evenly spaced steps: 1x → 0.7, 10x → 2.4, 100x → 4.6, 300x → 5.7. Now every size of line gets a fair say.

Part 4 The model: how it learnt and how it was tested

Notebook 04_modeling.ipynb (scripts: src/models/train.py, src/models/evaluate.py).

14. Model training, step by step

In simple words

The model is a student. Old IPOs are its practice questions with answers. It practises on old years, then sits an exam on newer years it has never seen. If it does well on the exam, we trust it a bit. If it only does well on practice questions, it just memorised them.

#What I didHow (step by step)Why (step by step)
1Kept the newest years aside
  1. 2010 to 2023 = practice (432 IPOs).
  2. 2024 to 2026 = final exam (202 IPOs).
  3. Nothing about the exam is used to choose anything.
  1. If you see the exam paper while studying, your marks are fake.
  2. In real life the model always predicts the future from the past.
2Practice tests by year (year folds)
  1. Learn from everything before 2019, test on 2019.
  2. Learn from everything before 2020, test on 2020.
  3. ... up to 2023. Five practice tests.
  4. Also leave out the last 7 days before each test year.
  1. The class helper regression_eval uses KFold(shuffle=True): it mixes years, so it would learn from 2023 to predict 2019 (the future).
  2. The 7-day gap: market features look 7 days back, so an IPO on 3 Jan must not be judged by a model that saw one from 30 Dec.
3Two simple baselines
  1. Median: always guess the median gain of all past IPOs.
  2. Bucket median: guess the median gain of past IPOs with the same subscription bucket (<1x, 1-3x, 3-10x, 10-30x, 30-100x, 100x+).
  1. The bucket median is what an experienced investor does by eye.
  2. If ML can't beat it, ML is not worth it.
4Three ML models
  1. Ridge: a straight-line model.
  2. Random Forest: 400 decision trees that vote.
  3. LightGBM: trees built one after another, each fixing the last one's mistakes.
  4. Missing values filled with the median inside a pipeline.
  1. Ridge is the simple yardstick and handles correlated columns.
  2. Trees catch combinations like "high QIB and happy market".
  3. Filling inside the pipeline means the median comes only from training years.
5First try: checked overfitting
  1. Trained each model with default-ish settings.
  2. Measured error on the practice years (train) and on the test year (valid), in one table.
  1. Train error much lower than valid error = the model memorised (overfitting).
  2. See the table below.
6Tuned settings
  1. A small grid of settings per model, 94 combinations in all.
  2. Also tried: +3 "vs last year" features, and giving old years less weight.
  3. Picked the setting with the lowest average miss (MAE) over 2019 to 2023.
  1. Small grid = less chance of a lucky winner.
  2. Choosing on 2019 to 2023 keeps the 2024 to 2026 exam clean.
7Exam 1: froze the model at the end of 2023
  1. Trained once on 2010 to 2023.
  2. Scored on 2024 to 2026.
  3. Result: every ML model lost to the bucket median.
  1. To see what happens if you never update the model.
  2. Kept on purpose: it showed a real problem (step 8).
8Found why: subscription inflation
  1. Same subscription bucket, three eras (EDA finding 7).
  2. 100x IPOs: 75% median gain in 2020 to 2023, 36.5% in 2024 to 2026.
  1. A model frozen in 2023 still expects the 2021 frenzy.
  2. Nobody would use a model for 3 years without updating it anyway.
9Exam 2: retrain every quarter (walk-forward)
  1. For each quarter from 2019: learn from all IPOs that listed before (quarter start − 7 days).
  2. Predict that quarter's IPOs.
  3. Move to the next quarter and repeat.
  1. This is exactly how it would be used in real life.
  2. Each prediction only ever saw the past.
10Picked Random Forest
  1. Lowest miss on 2019 to 2023 walk-forward (16.13 pp).
  2. Picked before looking at 2024 to 2026.
  1. The exam years must not take part in choosing.
11Predicted a range, not one number
  1. Three LightGBM models: a low guess (10th percentile), middle (50th), high (90th).
  2. They were too confident: only 56 to 67% of results fell inside instead of 80%.
  3. Fixed with rolling conformal calibration: look at how far the last 60 results fell outside their ranges, and widen the next range by that much.
  1. A single guess hides how unsure we are.
  2. A range that says 80% must really catch about 80%.
  3. After the fix: 78% and 79%.
12Explained every prediction
  1. Feature importance from the forest.
  2. SHAP values: for each IPO, how many percentage points each feature added or removed.
  1. An investor should see why: "the long QIB line added this many points, the weak market took away this many".
  2. The app's "Investment thesis" comes from SHAP.

15. How the model is scored

In simple words

MAE: on average, how far off is the guess? If the real jump is 20% and the model said 12%, it missed by 8. Average all the misses: that is MAE. Smaller is better.

Spearman: line up all the IPOs from best to worst by the guess, then by the real result. If the two lines look alike, the model is good at ordering, even if each exact number is off. 1 = perfect order, 0 = random.

First question: regression or classification?
RegressionClassification
What is predicteda numbera category (yes / no)
Our targetlisting gain in % (e.g. +95.6). So this is regression.–
Its measuresMAE, RMSE, R²accuracy, precision, recall, F1
Every measure used, with Random Forest's walk-forward numbers on 2024 to 2026
MeasureWhat it measures, in plain wordsOur numberRole
MAEaverage miss, in percentage points19.52 ppMain measure. Not ruled by a few 200% IPOs.
Median AEmiss on a typical IPO12.13 ppShows the typical miss is smaller than the average
RMSElike MAE, but big misses count extra27.99 ppReported, not used to choose: a few hot IPOs dominate it
R²share of the ups and downs the model explains0.56 (valid, year folds)Used in the train vs valid table

Part 5 Money: would following the model have paid?

Notebook 05_backtest.ipynb and src/forward_test.py.

18. Backtest: does it make money?

In simple words

Applying for an IPO is like buying a raffle ticket. If 15 people want the prize for every 1 prize, you win only 1 time in 15. So a super-popular IPO (100x) may jump a lot, but you almost never get it. A boring IPO jumps less, but you actually get it. The best plan is not "only the most popular ones", it's "skip the ones likely to fall".

A. The setup

Whoa normal (retail) investor
How much1 lot per IPO, about ₹15,000
When they sellat the opening price on listing day
Chance of getting shares1 ÷ retail subscription (100% if retail ≤ 1x)
Expected profit of one applicationlisting gain × ₹15,000 × chance of getting shares
Example: IRCTC95.6% × ₹15,000 = ₹14,344 if you get shares; chance 1 in 14.94 → expected ₹960
Fair testuses the walk-forward guesses (made before listing); the threshold is chosen on 2019 to 2023 only

B. The strategies compared

StrategyRuleThreshold picked on 2019 to 2023
Apply to every IPOalways apply–
The popular ruleapply only if 30x or more subscribed–
Tuned subscription cutoffapply if subscription ≥ best cutoff0x (= apply to everything)
Bucket medianapply if the bucket median ≥ best threshold−10% (= apply to everything)
Follow the modelapply if the model's guess ≥ best threshold−2%

What I sawThe 30x rule has the best hit rate (89.8%) but the worst profit: you expect only about 5 allotments from 98 applications. The model applies widely and skips the IPOs it expects to fall.
Careful"Expected profit" is an average over the lottery, not money someone actually made. Brokerage and tax are ignored (small for 1 lot).

D. Is the edge real or luck? (bootstrap)

In simple words

Put all 202 IPOs in a bag. Pull out 202 with your eyes closed, putting each one back after (so some come twice, some never). Check who wins. Do it 10,000 times. If the model wins almost every time, it's not luck.

Model vsExtra profit95% range of the extra profitModel loses inVerdict
Apply to every IPO₹6,082₹1,241 to ₹11,9780.4%real edge
Only if 30x+₹9,083−₹10,927 to ₹28,82118.5%not proven

E. What did the model skip?

In 2024 to 2026 the model skipped 15 IPOs: 9 listed below the offer price, 1 flat and 5 above (the best only +5.6%). All 15 had low subscription (1.0x to 3.2x).

F. Does it only work at exactly −2%?

  • 2019 to 2023: spiky. Anything from −4% to 0% beats applying to everything; +1% and above does not. So the exact −2% should not be over-read.
  • 2024 to 2026: every threshold from −5% to about +17% beats applying to everything, and the best would have been about +2%. The −2% (picked on older years) was on the safe side, not lucky.
Say it: "The 30x rule picks winners but you almost never get allotted. The model only skips the likely losers, and earned ₹30,588 against ₹24,506 for applying to everything; the bootstrap says that edge is real."

20. The app: Primary Desk

In simple words

The app is the guessing machine with a nice face. You type in a new IPO's line lengths, press a button, and it says SUBSCRIBE or AVOID, how much it expects, the bad case and the good case, and why.

Research NotePick a past IPO or type a new one → verdict, conviction, expected gain, bear and bull case (80% range), chance of allotment, expected value of one lot, the drivers for and against (SHAP), key risks, and the 5 most similar past IPOs. Part 7 Interview kit

What to say, what you may be asked, and the numbers people get wrong.

21. Say it in 1 minute

"I built a model that predicts an Indian IPO's listing-day gain the moment subscription closes. I took 652 real IPOs from Kaggle, matched each one to its NSE symbol, and checked Kaggle's listing prices against the NSE open from Yahoo, after fixing Yahoo's split adjustment: 95% agreed. EDA showed subscription is the strongest signal, but it has inflated over time, so a model trained once and frozen failed on 2024 to 2026. I switched to retraining every quarter. The random forest ranks IPOs best (Spearman 0.71 on unseen years), though a simple subscription lookup is as good on the exact number, which I report openly. Its real value is the apply / skip call: following it, a retail investor's expected profit was ₹30,588 vs ₹24,506 for applying to everything, and a bootstrap shows that edge is real. A one-time forward test on 78 newer IPOs told the same story. It all runs in a Streamlit app that gives a Subscribe / Avoid call with a calibrated 80% range and the reasons."

22. Questions you may get

Tap a question to see the answer.

Why not use a normal random train_test_split?

IPOs come in waves and subscription has inflated. A random split would train on 2025 and test on 2019, which leaks the future and gives a fake score. I split by time: tune on 2010 to 2023, test on 2024 to 2026, and retrain every quarter.

Why didn't you use the class helper regression_eval?

It uses KFold with shuffle=True, which mixes years. I kept the same idea (one table of train vs valid MAE and R²) but with year folds, and a 7-day gap between training and validation.

Why not use GMP (grey market premium)? Everyone looks at it.

It is unofficial, quoted by informal dealers, and there is no reliable, checkable history of it. A model trained on numbers I can't verify would not be trustworthy. Everything I used comes from official or checkable sources.

Your model loses to a simple lookup on MAE. So why use it?

On the exact number, yes, the bucket median is as good or slightly better (17.3 vs 19.5 pp in 2024 to 2026). But the model ranks IPOs better (Spearman 0.71 vs 0.67), and the decision "apply or skip" is a ranking question. In the backtest the model made more expected profit than every simple rule. I report both, honestly.

Is your model overfitting?

I checked with a train vs valid table. Untuned trees missed by ~4 pp on training years and ~15 pp on new years, so I limited tree depth and leaf size, which shrank the gap (~7 vs ~15). Every score I quote is on years the model never saw, and a forward test on 78 later IPOs gave similar results (Spearman 0.72), which an overfit model would not.

How do you know there is no data leakage?

Market data stops 7 days before listing; CMP / current-gain columns were dropped; folds keep a 7-day gap; walk-forward only trains on IPOs listed before each quarter; missing values are filled inside the pipeline; and an automated test checks that adding later IPOs never changes an earlier IPO's features.

You must apply before subscription closes. How can the model use the final subscription?

By the evening of the last day the subscription numbers are almost final, and that is when most people apply. The app takes the last-day numbers. The market data is from 7 days earlier, so it is safely in the past either way.

Why MAE and not R² or RMSE?

The target has a long right tail: a few IPOs jump 150 to 250%. RMSE and R² are dominated by those few. MAE is the average miss in percentage points, which is easy to explain. For the decision I also use Spearman, which measures ranking.

Why Random Forest and not LightGBM?

It had the lowest MAE on the 2019 to 2023 walk-forward (16.13 vs 16.23), and I picked it before looking at 2024 to 2026. It also turned out best on ranking in 2024 to 2026. LightGBM is still used for the 80% range (quantile loss).

Why did you keep outliers?

They are real IPOs: 300x subscriptions and ₹20,000+ crore issues really happened, and they are the most important ones to get right. I used a log scale and MAE so they don't dominate.

What is conformal calibration?

The quantile models said "80% range" but only caught 56 to 67%. Rolling conformal looks at how far the last 60 results fell outside their ranges and widens the next range by that amount. After it, the range caught 78 to 79%, and 87% in the forward test.

How is the allotment lottery handled?

Expected profit = gain × ₹15,000 × (1 ÷ retail subscription). That is why the 30x rule has the best hit rate (89.8%) but the worst profit: you get about 5 allotments from 98 applications.

Is the profit difference just luck?

Paired bootstrap, 10,000 resamples: against applying to everything, the extra ₹6,082 has a 95% range of ₹1,241 to ₹11,978 (model loses in 0.4%), so it's real. Against the 30x rule it is not proven (range crosses zero).

How did you check the data is right?

I matched every IPO to NSE, took the NSE opening price from Yahoo, fixed Yahoo's split adjustment (IRCTC's ₹626 showed as ~₹125), and compared: 95% of checkable IPOs agree within 10 pp. Where they disagreed, I checked by hand against news (CDSL, Paras Defence, Nazara, Bansal Wire): Kaggle was right.

What would you do next?

Add "no depth limit" to the forest's tuning grid (it scored slightly better on validation); add more pre-listing information such as the company's financials and sector; get actual allotment ratios instead of the 1 ÷ subscription estimate; and keep adding new IPOs so the model stays current.

24. Limits

In simple words

Every machine has things it can't do. Saying them first shows you understand your own work.

LimitWhat it means
Exact gain is hardAverage miss ~16 to 20 pp. A simple subscription lookup is as good on the exact number. The value is ranking.
The market keeps changingSubscription has inflated. The model only adapts as new IPOs are added and it is retrained.
Allotment odds are estimated1 ÷ retail subscription is an approximation; real odds depend on how many people apply for more than one lot.
Costs ignoredBrokerage, tax and slippage are not in the profit (small for 1 lot).
135 targets unverifiedMostly old (2010 to 2011) IPOs not on NSE's list any more; kept with Kaggle's number, marked.
History ends 4 Nov 2026Newer IPOs must be added for the "recent IPO" features to stay current.
Not investment adviceA study project. GMP and company financials are not used.
